claim: The helical centerline pitch and radius of wild-type H. pylori cells dictate surface curvatures of considerably higher positive and negative Gaussian curvatures than those present in straight- or curved-rod H. pylori.
source: The helical centerline pitch and radius of wild-type H. pylori cells dictate surface curvatures of considerably higher positive and negative Gaussian curvatures than those present in straight- or curved-rod H. pylori.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript, specifically the analysis of Gaussian curvature distributions shown in Figure 2.

claim: Quantitative 3D microscopy analysis of short pulses with either N-acetylmuramic acid or D-alanine metabolic probes showed that cell wall growth is enhanced at both sidewall curvature extremes.
source: Quantitative 3D microscopy analysis of short pulses with either N-acetylmuramic acid or D-alanine metabolic probes showed that cell wall growth is enhanced at both sidewall curvature extremes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from metabolic labeling experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: MreB is most abundant at negative Gaussian curvature.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed MreB is most abundant at negative Gaussian curvature, while the bactofilin CcmA is most abundant at positive Gaussian curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and curvature enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The bactofilin CcmA is most abundant at positive Gaussian curvature.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed MreB is most abundant at negative Gaussian curvature, while the bactofilin CcmA is most abundant at positive Gaussian curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and curvature enrichment analysis shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Strains expressing CcmA variants with altered polymerization properties lose helical shape and associated positive Gaussian curvatures.
source: Strains expressing CcmA variants with altered polymerization properties lose helical shape and associated positive Gaussian curvatures.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from CcmA point mutant strains shown in Figure 8.

claim: CcmA and MreB promote PG synthesis at positive and negative Gaussian curvatures, respectively.
source: We thus propose a model where CcmA and MreB promote PG synthesis at positive and negative Gaussian curvatures, respectively, and that this patterning is one mechanism necessary for maintaining helical shape.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of the H. pylori peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall (sacculus) is ultimately responsible for the shape of the cell.
source: As is the case for most bacteria (Höltje, 1998), the structure of the H. pylori peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall (sacculus) is ultimately responsible for the shape of the cell; purified cell walls maintain helical shape (Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to general bacterial knowledge (Höltje, 1998) and a specific citation about H. pylori (Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: Purified H. pylori cell walls maintain helical shape.
source: As is the case for most bacteria (Höltje, 1998), the structure of the H. pylori peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall (sacculus) is ultimately responsible for the shape of the cell; purified cell walls maintain helical shape (Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: Helical cell shape maintenance in H. pylori requires a suite of both PG-modifying enzymes (Csd1, Csd3/HdpA, Csd4, and Csd6) to remodel the cell wall.
source: Helical cell shape maintenance in H. pylori requires a suite of both PG-modifying enzymes (Csd1, Csd3/HdpA, Csd4, and Csd6) to remodel the cell wall and non-enzymatic proteins (Csd2, Csd5, CcmA, and Csd7) that may act as scaffolds or play other structural roles (Bonis et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2013; Sycuro et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bonis et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2013; Sycuro et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).

claim: Helical cell shape maintenance in H. pylori requires non-enzymatic proteins (Csd2, Csd5, CcmA, and Csd7) that may act as scaffolds or play other structural roles.
source: Helical cell shape maintenance in H. pylori requires a suite of both PG-modifying enzymes (Csd1, Csd3/HdpA, Csd4, and Csd6) to remodel the cell wall and non-enzymatic proteins (Csd2, Csd5, CcmA, and Csd7) that may act as scaffolds or play other structural roles (Bonis et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2013; Sycuro et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bonis et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2013; Sycuro et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).

claim: CcmA loss in H. pylori results in rod-shaped cells with minimal sidewall curvature.
source: CcmA loss in H. pylori results in rod-shaped cells with minimal sidewall curvature (Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: H. pylori CcmA has been shown to self-oligomerize.
source: As with other organisms, H. pylori CcmA has been shown to self-oligomerize (Holtrup et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Holtrup et al., 2019).

claim: CcmA was shown to co-purify with Csd5 and the PG biosynthetic enzyme MurF.
source: Recently CcmA was shown to co-purify with Csd5 and the PG biosynthetic enzyme MurF (Blair et al., 2018), suggesting CcmA may influence cell wall growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Blair et al., 2018).

claim: In the rod shaped Escherichia coli, MreB helps direct synthesis preferentially to sites at or below zero Gaussian curvature.
source: In the rod shaped Escherichia coli, MreB helps direct synthesis preferentially to sites at or below zero Gaussian curvature. One working model is that this growth pattern promotes rod shape by accelerating growth at dents and restricting growth at bulges along the sidewall, thereby enforcing diameter control (Bratton et al., 2018; Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bratton et al., 2018; Ursell et al., 2014).

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, MreB filaments have been shown to move in paths oriented approximately perpendicular to the long axis of rod shaped cells.
source: In the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis, MreB filaments have been shown to move in paths oriented approximately perpendicular to the long axis of rod shaped cells. The relative organization of path orientations decreases with an increase in rod diameter, suggesting that filament orientation is sensitive to changes in cell surface curvatures (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hussain et al., 2018).

claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long.
source: Wild-type cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long and 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter, have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm, and have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells are 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter.
source: Wild-type cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long and 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter, have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm, and have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm.
source: Wild-type cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long and 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter, have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm, and have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm.
source: Wild-type cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long and 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter, have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm, and have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claim: The average major to minor length ratio in H. pylori is 1.69 ± 0.16.
source: Using the simulated counterparts to these cells, we determined that the average major to minor length ratio is 1.69 ± 0.16, meaning that the major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3G.

claim: The major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis in H. pylori.
source: Using the simulated counterparts to these cells, we determined that the average major to minor length ratio is 1.69 ± 0.16, meaning that the major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3G.

claim: The average Gaussian curvature at the major axis is 5 ± 1 µm−2.
source: We also determined from the simulated cells that the average Gaussian curvature at the major axis is 5 ± 1 µm−2, and the average Gaussian curvature at the minor axis is −11 ± 4 µm−2 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3H.

claim: The average Gaussian curvature at the minor axis is −11 ± 4 µm−2.
source: We also determined from the simulated cells that the average Gaussian curvature at the major axis is 5 ± 1 µm−2, and the average Gaussian curvature at the minor axis is −11 ± 4 µm−2 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3H.

claim: Supplementation with 4 mg/ml MurNAc partially rescued growth of HJH1 in the presence of 50 µg/ml fosfomycin, but not the parental strain (LSH108).
source: Supplementation with 4 mg/ml MurNAc partially rescued growth of HJH1 in the presence of 50 µg/ml fosfomycin, but not the parental strain (LSH108) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MurNAc-alk is incorporated into H. pylori peptidoglycan.
source: To verify that clickable MurNAc-alk is indeed incorporated into the cell wall, we purified sacculi from HJH1 labeled with MurNAc-alk for six doublings for MS/MS analysis. We positively identified MurNAc-alk-pentapeptide and MurNAc-alk-tetra-pentapeptide, the most abundant monomeric and dimeric species in the H. pylori cell wall, (Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), as well as less-abundant species (Table 1), confirming incorporation.
evidence: The claim is supported by MS/MS data shown in Figure 4B, C and Table 1.

claim: D-Ala-alk is incorporated exclusively at the pentapeptide position in H. pylori peptidoglycan.
source: To verify that D-Ala-alk is incorporated into the cell wall and to determine the position(s) at which it is incorporated, we purified sacculi from wild-type (LSH100) cells labeled for six doublings for analysis. D-Ala-alk was detected in only pentapeptide monomers and tetra-pentapeptide dimers, indicating that D-Ala-alk is exclusively incorporated at the pentapeptide position (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC and MS data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: MreB is essential in LSH100 H. pylori strain.
source: Since multiple attempts to knock out mreB in wild-type LSH100 were unsuccessful, we generated IM4, a merodiploid strain with a second copy of mreB at a neutral intergenic locus (McGee locus Langford et al., 2006) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) for comparative transformation experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: MreB localization is depleted at the poles in H. pylori.
source: Curvature enrichment analysis of non-dividing cells confirmed that MreB localization is depleted at the poles (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: As Gaussian curvature became more negative, relative MreB concentration increased monotonically.
source: Regardless of whether the poles were included in the analysis, we observed that as Gaussian curvature became more negative, relative MreB concentration increased monotonically (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wild-type CcmA forms filaments of varying length, long helical bundles of filaments, and lattice structures in vitro.
source: Negative staining of recombinant wild-type CcmA purified from E. coli revealed filaments of varying length, long helical bundles of filaments, and lattice structures (Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8A-B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CcmA lattices have a filament spacing of 5.5 nm.
source: Fourier transform analysis of the lattice structures revealed a filament spacing of 5.5 nm (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), similar to that previously observed for C. crescentus BacA lattices (5.6 nm) (Vasa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fourier transform analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: CcmA lattices are skewed with an acute angle of 71.5° and an obtuse angle of 106.2°.
source: While BacA forms orthogonal lattices, the CcmA lattices are skewed (acute angle = 71.5°; obtuse angle = 106.2°).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fourier transform analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The I55A CcmA variant does not form ordered structures in vitro.
source: While both proteins could be expressed and purified from E. coli (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), the recombinant proteins either fail to form any higher order structures under any buffer condition tested (I55A; Figure 8C) or form no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro (L110S; Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The L110S CcmA variant forms no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro.
source: While both proteins could be expressed and purified from E. coli (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), the recombinant proteins either fail to form any higher order structures under any buffer condition tested (I55A; Figure 8C) or form no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro (L110S; Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both I55A and L110S CcmA mutant strains displayed a morphology indistinguishable from a ccmA null strain.
source: In both cases, the mutant strains displayed a morphology indistinguishable from a ccmA null strain (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that formation of higher-order structures by CcmA may be necessary for cell shape-determining functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell shape analysis data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Wild-type CcmA localizes at the cell boundary as puncta and short arcs and is largely absent from the center of the cell.
source: Wild-type CcmA was observed at the cell boundary as puncta and short arcs and was largely absent from the center of the cell, indicating an association with the cell membrane (Figure 9D and Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The mutant CcmA proteins (I55A and L110S) localized as puncta at the center with minimal signal at the cell boundary.
source: In contrast to cells expressing the wild-type version of CcmA, the mutant CcmA proteins localized as puncta at the center with minimal signal at the cell boundary (Figure 9G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9G-J.

claim: CcmA has a marked preference for the positive helical axis area.
source: With or without the poles, we saw a marked preference for the positive helical axis area (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1, red line and shaded box) that overlapped with the positive curvature enrichment peaks of MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no distinguishable curvature preference for I55A or L110S CcmA compared to preimmune serum.
source: There was no distinguishable curvature preference for I55A or L110S CcmA compared to preimmune serum (Figure 10—figure supplement 3A, red and dark red vs. dotted light pink and dotted mauve, respectively), indicating that these proteins are unable to localize preferentially to positive Gaussian surface curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In ΔccmA cells, MreB curvature preference appears largely similar to wild-type with poles excluded.
source: MreB curvature preference appears largely similar in both wild-type (HJH1, amgK murU, light pink) and ΔccmA with poles excluded (JTH6, amgK murU ΔccmA, dark pink) (Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: In ΔccmA cells, MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk patterning change with loss of CcmA; there is greater relative enrichment at low magnitude negative Gaussian curvature compared to wild-type cells.
source: In contrast, MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk patterning change with loss of CcmA; there is greater relative enrichment at low magnitude negative Gaussian curvature in ΔccmA cells (dark green and dark blue) compared to wild-type cells (light green and light blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: In ΔccmA cells, the enrichment at positive Gaussian curvature is both less pronounced and shifted to lower Gaussian curvature than that of wild-type.
source: Additionally, in ΔccmA cells the enrichment at positive Gaussian curvature is both less pronounced and shifted to lower Gaussian curvature than that of wild-type (Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H. pylori is a helical Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the human stomach.
source: Helicobacter pylori is a helical Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the human stomach and can cause stomach ulcers and gastric cancers (Correa, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Correa, 1988) and represents established knowledge.

claim: H. pylori can cause stomach ulcers and gastric cancers.
source: Helicobacter pylori is a helical Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the human stomach and can cause stomach ulcers and gastric cancers (Correa, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Correa, 1988).

claim: H. pylori is a genetically tractable organism with a compact genome that minimizes redundancy.
source: H. pylori is a main model organism for studying helical cell shape, in part because it is a genetically tractable organism with a compact genome that minimizes redundancy (Tomb et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Tomb et al., 1997).

claim: Bactofilins are bacteria-specific cytoskeletal proteins with diverse functions.
source: Bactofilins are bacteria-specific cytoskeletal proteins with diverse functions, including playing a role in stalk elongation in Caulobacter crescentus (Kühn et al., 2010) and helical pitch modulation in Leptospira biflexa (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kühn et al., 2010; Jackson et al., 2018).

claim: Bactofilins play a role in stalk elongation in Caulobacter crescentus.
source: Bactofilins are bacteria-specific cytoskeletal proteins with diverse functions, including playing a role in stalk elongation in Caulobacter crescentus (Kühn et al., 2010) and helical pitch modulation in Leptospira biflexa (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Kühn et al., 2010).

claim: Bactofilins play a role in helical pitch modulation in Leptospira biflexa.
source: Bactofilins are bacteria-specific cytoskeletal proteins with diverse functions, including playing a role in stalk elongation in Caulobacter crescentus (Kühn et al., 2010) and helical pitch modulation in Leptospira biflexa (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jackson et al., 2018).

claim: The curved-rod shaped Proteobacteria Caulobacter crescentus and Vibrio cholerae limit relative levels of PG synthesis at negative curvatures through the action of long, cell-spanning cytoskeletal filaments (CreS and CrvA).
source: To be able to maintain curvature in the presence of MreB, the curved-rod shaped Gram-negative Proteobacteria Caulobacter crescentus and Vibrio cholerae appear to limit relative levels of PG synthesis at negative curvatures through the action of long, cell-spanning cytoskeletal filaments (CreS and CrvA) that preferentially localize to the minor axis (negative Gaussian curvature) and enable cells to increase relative synthesis rates on the opposite side of the wall (positive Gaussian curvature) (Bartlett et al., 2017; Cabeen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bartlett et al., 2017; Cabeen et al., 2009).

claim: CreS and CrvA preferentially localize to the minor axis (negative Gaussian curvature) in C. crescentus and V. cholerae.
source: To be able to maintain curvature in the presence of MreB, the curved-rod shaped Gram-negative Proteobacteria Caulobacter crescentus and Vibrio cholerae appear to limit relative levels of PG synthesis at negative curvatures through the action of long, cell-spanning cytoskeletal filaments (CreS and CrvA) that preferentially localize to the minor axis (negative Gaussian curvature) and enable cells to increase relative synthesis rates on the opposite side of the wall (positive Gaussian curvature) (Bartlett et al., 2017; Cabeen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bartlett et al., 2017; Cabeen et al., 2009).

claim: H. pylori does not have any known functional L-D-transpeptidases.
source: H. pylori does not have any known functional L-D-transpeptidases and no detectable 3–3 crosslinks, a hallmark of L-D-transpeptidase activity (Costa et al., 1999; Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Costa et al., 1999; Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: H. pylori has no detectable 3–3 crosslinks, a hallmark of L-D-transpeptidase activity.
source: H. pylori does not have any known functional L-D-transpeptidases and no detectable 3–3 crosslinks, a hallmark of L-D-transpeptidase activity (Costa et al., 1999; Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Costa et al., 1999; Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: H. pylori has a pentapeptide-rich cell wall.
source: H. pylori has a pentapeptide-rich cell wall and it is unclear if H pylori actively regulates pentapeptide trimming.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about H. pylori cell wall composition.

claim: The cell shape determining protein Csd3/HdpA has been shown to have weak pentapeptide carboxypeptidase activity in vitro.
source: However, the cell shape determining protein Csd3/HdpA has been shown to have weak pentapeptide carboxypeptidase activity in vitro (Bonis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Bonis et al., 2010).

claim: The bactofilins BacA and BacB in C. crescentus recruit the PG synthase PBPC to assist in stalk elongation.
source: In support of this hypothesis, the bactofilins BacA and BacB in C. crescentus recruit the PG synthase PBPC to assist in stalk elongation, indicating that they help recruit PG synthesis (Kühn et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Kühn et al., 2010).

claim: Loss of CcmA results in an increased degree of crosslinking in the sacculus.
source: It is possible that CcmA may also help promote localized crosslink trimming, as loss of CcmA results in an increased degree of crosslinking in the sacculus (Sycuro et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Sycuro et al., 2010).

claim: The bactofilin LbbD modulates helical pitch in the spirochete Leptospira biflexa.
source: While it remains unclear how filament or lattice twist would be coupled to cell wall twist, the bactofilin LbbD modulates helical pitch in the spirochete Leptospira biflexa (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jackson et al., 2018).

claim: Fosfomycin blocks the first committed step in PG precursor synthesis by preventing the conversion of UDP-GlcNAc into UDP-MurNAc.
source: Fosfomycin blocks the first committed step in PG precursor synthesis by preventing the conversion of UDP-GlcNAc into UDP-MurNAc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about fosfomycin's mechanism of action, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of fosfomycin for strain HJH1 is 25 µg/ml.
source: We determined the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of fosfomycin of our strain to be 25 µg/ml (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dimensions of H. pylori cells (1.5–3.5 µm in length and 0.45 µm in diameter) are near the limit of light microscopy resolution.
source: Since the dimensions of H. pylori cells (1.5–3.5 µm in length and 0.45 µm in diameter Figure 3) are near the limit of light microscopy resolution, we employed 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) to more clearly resolve cells in three dimensions (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about light microscopy resolution limits and the measured dimensions of H. pylori cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) was employed to more clearly resolve H. pylori cells in three dimensions.
source: Since the dimensions of H. pylori cells (1.5–3.5 µm in length and 0.45 µm in diameter Figure 3) are near the limit of light microscopy resolution, we employed 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) to more clearly resolve cells in three dimensions (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described and images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Helical cells have a multimodal distribution of sidewall Gaussian curvature that includes an apparent peak at negative curvature and another at positive curvature.
source: Rather than having a unimodal distribution, helical cells have a multimodal distribution that includes an apparent peak at negative curvature and another at positive curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Gaussian curvature distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Changing cell length had a negligible impact on the distribution of surface curvatures along the sidewall.
source: Changing cell length had a negligible impact on the distribution of surface curvatures along the sidewall (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Decreasing the pitch resulted in a helix with tighter coils and a greater distance between the peak of negative and positive Gaussian surface curvatures.
source: Decreasing the pitch resulted in a helix with tighter coils and a greater distance between the peak of negative and positive Gaussian surface curvatures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Increasing the helical diameter resulted in cells that looked less like straight-rod cells and had a greater distance between the peak of negative and positive Gaussian surface curvatures.
source: Increasing the helical diameter resulted in cells that looked less like straight-rod cells and had a greater distance between the peak of negative and positive Gaussian surface curvatures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Cells had a greater proportion of sidewall area with positive Gaussian curvature than with negative.
source: In holding with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, cells had a greater proportion of sidewall area with positive Gaussian curvature than with negative, and the magnitude of the positive Gaussian curvature was less than that of the negative Gaussian curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and is consistent with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.

claim: The magnitude of the positive Gaussian curvature was less than that of the negative Gaussian curvature.
source: In holding with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, cells had a greater proportion of sidewall area with positive Gaussian curvature than with negative, and the magnitude of the positive Gaussian curvature was less than that of the negative Gaussian curvature.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and is consistent with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.

claim: For both MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk metabolic probes, signal was largely absent from the poles.
source: Curvature enrichment analysis of whole cell surfaces revealed that for both metabolic probes, signal was largely absent from the poles, as seen by the drop-off of relative enrichment at curvatures above 10 µm−2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MurNAc-alk was enriched at two sites: at negative curvature, enrichment increases as curvature becomes more negative; at positive curvature, enrichment peaks near 6 µm−2 and then begins to decrease at higher curvatures.
source: Looking at sidewall curvature alone, MurNAc-alk was enriched at two sites. At negative curvature, enrichment increases as curvature becomes more negative. At positive curvature, enrichment peaks near 6 µm−2 and then begins to decrease at higher curvatures (Figure 6C, green).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: D-Ala-alk showed peaks of enrichment aligning with those of MurNAc-alk, but the magnitude of the peak at positive curvature was reduced.
source: D-Ala-alk showed peaks of enrichment aligning with those of MurNAc-alk (Figure 6C, blue), but the magnitude of the peak at positive curvature was reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The mock labeling control showed minimal curvature bias.
source: The mock labeling control showed minimal curvature bias and is on average 3.6% of the D-Ala-alk signal and 4.5% of the MurNAc-alk signal (Figure 6B and C, gray and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: MreB is present at the cell periphery as many individual foci and some short arcs that appear to be oriented approximately circumferentially and excluded from the poles.
source: Immunofluorescence labeling with 3D SIM imaging revealed that MreB is present at the cell periphery as many individual foci and some short arcs that appear to be oriented approximately circumferentially and excluded from the poles (Figure 7B,D and E and Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B, D, E.

claim: Preimmune serum signal was 36.4% of the MreB signal.
source: Preimmune serum signal was 36.4% of the MreB signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), but did not show a curvature preference (Figure 7E, gray).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Preimmune serum did not show a curvature preference.
source: Preimmune serum signal was 36.4% of the MreB signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), but did not show a curvature preference (Figure 7E, gray).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The wild-type (no FLAG) negative control was 28.9% of the CcmA-FLAG signal.
source: The wild-type (no FLAG) negative control was 28.9% of the CcmA-FLAG signal (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2B.
